title: Democrats distance themselves from trans rights – close midterm races may show whether that pays off
paragraphs: A wave of anti-transgender legislation has appeared in statehouses across the country over the past few years. Now, transgender issues are a recurring topic on the 2026 midterm campaign trail.

As a scholar of LGBTQ+ politics and history, I’ve noticed surprising trends in how Democrats in key states like Texas and Ohio talk about policies focused on transgender people, as the party vies for control of Congress.

With a rise in anti-trans rhetoric from the White House, some Democrats are using similar messaging in an attempt to secure undecided voters. In my assessment, this approach could alienate moderates, progressives and LGBTQ+ people more broadly.
Democratic candidates have split sharply on transition-related care and inclusion in school sports.

In Massachusetts, Rep. Seth Moulton came out against transgender girls competing in school sports, just days after President Donald Trump’s victory in November 2024. But Sen. Ed Markey, Moulton’s primary opponent for the Senate seat, took the opposite approach, stating his unwavering support for transgender rights.

Markey polled ahead of Moulton throughout 2026 and won the primary by nearly 30 percentage points. Public opinion data shows that two-thirds of Democratic likely primary voters in Massachusetts said they would be less likely to back a candidate who opposes transgender rights.

Other Democrats, especially in Southern and Midwestern states, are taking a more conservative approach to transgender rights. In Texas, Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico has reversed his past support for transgender athletes.

Months after his March primary victory against Rep. Jasmine Crockett, Talarico said in a Fox News interview that he would “oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness.”
According to scholars and media watchdog groups like GLAAD, appeals to “safety” and “fairness” are common anti-trans dog whistles that perpetuate misinformation about transgender athletes.

The shift has not resulted in a polling bump for Talarico in his race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Polls of likely voters from July to early September gave Talarico an average lead of 3.16 percentage points. Polls since mid-September put his average lead at 2.66 percentage points.

Republican-aligned super PACs are also emphasizing transgender issues. Elon Musk’s America PAC has spent US$100 million on anti-trans ads in battleground states like Texas, Ohio and Alaska. Some of these ads feature people implied to be transgender women, though it is unclear whether they were actors or AI-generated.
With the prevalence of anti-trans ads, Democratic campaigns are responding in different ways. Some are veering to the right by mirroring GOP positions, like transgender exclusion from school sports.

Ohio offers clear examples of this gamble. In June, the state’s Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Amy Acton, made an anti-trans comment, referring to transgender girls as “boys.” This quickly drew criticism from statewide LGBTQ+ groups and community leaders.

In Ohio’s 9th congressional district, Rep. Marcy Kaptur’s campaign has run multiple anti-trans ads focusing on parental rights and transgender children in school sports, saying that the congresswoman voted to keep “transgender ideology” out of schools. The campaign also recently ran mailers with this message.

Kaptur’s county party condemned the ads, saying they were “disappointed and ashamed” of her campaign. When the state party’s Pride Caucus shared the county party’s statement on social media, the post was deleted. Pride Caucus members accused state party leadership of censorship; weeks later, transgender leaders from the caucus resigned in protest.

In contrast, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is running against Republican Sen. Jon Husted, has focused his campaign ads on affordability, data center regulations and the Epstein files without wavering on his support for transgender rights, as Acton and Kaptur have.
After a misleading super PAC ad about transgender healthcare from the GOP’s Senate Leadership Fund, Brown’s campaign released a counter ad correcting the claim before pivoting to affordability.

Days later, the same GOP super PAC released another ad targeting Brown. Reporting has confirmed that the ad, which features an adult from Texas rather than Ohio, is factually inaccurate and misleading.

Recent polling suggests Brown is outperforming his fellow Democrat Acton, who is running for governor, by 2 percentage points. While these polls don’t isolate the effect of a single issue, Acton has faced criticism from the public, in addition to state and national LGBTQ+ organizations.

Amid rising prices on fuel and food, upticks in unemployment and a national hiring slowdown, consumer confidence in the economy has dropped to its lowest point in over a decade. Nationally, many Democrats are trying to emphasize these points. To counter that message, some Republicans continue to emphasize “culture war” issues like transgender rights.

Currently, Democrats outperform Republicans on the generic congressional ballot – a polling tool that asks voters which party they’d back without naming candidates. But messaging on transgender rights may be a tipping point for midterm voters.

As a growing electorate of 12% of the U.S. adult population and with a voter turnout rate of roughly 80%, LGBTQ+ people are a strong voting bloc. Recent polling indicates that two-thirds of LGBTQ+ adults said they would be extremely to somewhat comfortable with trans athletes competing on sports teams that don’t match their sex at birth.

In battleground states, anti-trans messages could cost votes and spell defeat for Democrats who rely on them. The risk is especially high in states like Ohio and Texas, where races are close and LGBTQ+ adults are estimated to make up more than 11% of the adult population.

In Texas, Talarico’s lead could be undone by depressed turnout among the Lone Star State’s 2.24 million LGBTQ+ adults. In Ohio, home to roughly 883,000 LGBTQ+ adults, Acton’s gubernatorial race and Kaptur’s congressional district race are both statistical ties.

title: More than 119 million Brazilians voted in the Oct. 4 election – including about 21,000 Florida residents
paragraphs: More than 119 million Brazilians voted on Oct. 4, 2026, in the national elections to select the country’s next president and the governors of all 27 states, among other government officials.
That’s nearly 75% of the approximately 159 million eligible voters. Unlike in the U.S., voting is mandatory in Brazil for all citizens between the ages of 18 and 70.
This includes nearly 1 million Brazilians who currently live outside the country. About 265,000 Brazilians call the U.S. home, with small but growing communities in Boston, New York and Miami.

Because neither incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nor his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of disgraced former President Jair Bolsonaro, managed to get over 50% of the votes, Brazilians at home and abroad will have to turn out again on Oct. 25 for a runoff election.

Brazil does not have a long tradition of democracy. But it does have a secure and sophisticated election system. As a scholar of Latin American history and politics, and a Brazilian citizen living in the U.S., I watched these elections with great interest.

Brazilians living abroad are required by law to vote, but they may not cast ballots by mail or online. In many countries, Brazilian consulates serve as the polling places for the diaspora population. Because the U.S. is so spread out, the Brazilian government sets up 15 polling places in 12 states. Two of these are in Florida – one in the Orlando area, where about 26,000 Brazilian voters live, and one in Miami, which is home to the third-largest concentration of Brazilians in the U.S., with more than 40,000 registered voters.

Voting takes place in a single day – always a Sunday – through electronic voting machines, and results are known within a few hours. Though it is compulsory, the penalty for not voting is just a small fine – about US$1 – and as long as a citizen notifies the government within two months of the election that they did not vote, they remain in good legal standing.
So it’s not surprising that only about 75,000 Brazilians – roughly 28% of eligible voters – cast their ballots in the U.S. on Oct. 4.

It’s unclear whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations prevented people from voting, though some Brazilians say they believe fear of ICE contributed to a lower turnout than in 2022, when more than 37% of eligible voters cast their ballots. Organizations for expats in the U.S. warned Brazilians that if their immigration status was precarious, they should not vote.

What is clear is the importance of this election for the future of Latin America’s largest economy and society, as well as for the future of Brazil-U.S. relations. If reelected, Lula is likely to continue to resist overt pressures from Washington to weaken Brazil’s economic ties with China.

On the other hand, Flávio Bolsonaro has signaled that he plans to have much closer relations with the U.S. That is why President Donald Trump would prefer to have a Bolsonaro in power, so that the U.S. influence in Latin America may be further consolidated.

Among Brazilian voters who were abroad on Election Day, Lula won in 64 out of 101 countries where voting was made available by Brazilian diplomatic authorities. But Flávio Bolsonaro won in some of the nations with the largest numbers of Brazilian residents. This includes the U.S., Japan and neighboring countries in South America.

In the U.S., Brazilian voters cast 45,004 ballots for Flávio Bolsonaro and 23,335 for Lula. This seems to be another indication of the polarization that has shaped this key election and, more broadly, the general political context of Brazil in the past few years.
I was not surprised to see that Flávio Bolsonaro finished in the lead on Oct. 4, as the electoral pendulum across the region has been swinging to the right of the political spectrum for some time.

Even though Lula managed to defeat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, Bolsonarismo – the extreme-right political movement that carries his name – has remained the most influential political force in the country. This is a right-wing movement whose leaders, especially members of the Bolsonaro family, have openly and consistently called for the revival of Brazil’s military regime that ruled the country from the mid-1960s to mid-1980s.

Now that Flávio Bolsonaro, an otherwise irrelevant senator from the state of Rio de Janeiro, where the staunch political base of the Bolsonaros is located, has finished ahead of Lula in the first round of elections, it seems clear that the extreme right has the upper hand in Brazil today.
A few years ago, Brazil seemed on track to becoming a mature democracy, after having held several electoral cycles with peaceful transfers of power to opposition candidates.
But now, considering the lack of commitment to democratic traditions in the Bolsonarismo movement, this trend risks being derailed, ironically, by means of a democratic election.

title: Pardoning of Israeli soldier evokes a long history of clemency for those who kill Palestinians
paragraphs: The pardoning of Elor Azaria, a former Israeli soldier convicted of killing a wounded Palestinian man in the occupied West Bank, comes with a history.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s decision itself – announced on Sept. 19, 2026 – came more than eight years after Azaria left prison.
The immediate effect is that it clears Azaria of his criminal record. But its public significance is broader – and reaches much further back.

I study how Israelis have talked about Palestinian lives and deaths over the past century. In my forthcoming book, I trace a recurring idea: Palestinians are viewed as an obstacle to Israel’s territorial and security goals, and whose removal can be imagined as necessary or justified. Azaria’s pardon fits into this notion, showing how the state’s response to killing Palestinians can be expressed through the language of mercy for the perpetrator – and it is a pattern that goes back almost 80 years.

The details of Azaria’s case are fairly straightforward. On March 24, 2016, Abdel Fattah al-Sharif and another Palestinian armed with knives attacked an Israeli soldier in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank. Al-Sharif was shot and lay wounded on the ground. Minutes later, Azaria approached and shot him in the head.
Video of the killing circulated widely. An Israeli military court convicted Azaria of manslaughter in 2017 and sentenced him to 18 months in prison. He was released after serving nine months.
Justifying his decision, Herzog’s office cited the years that had passed, Azaria’s expression of sorrow in his application for a pardon, and the approach of Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement.
Yet Azaria had said after his release that he would act the same way again. While the conviction will remain part of the historical record, the pardon removes any lasting consequence for him.
Herzog’s decision was warmly received by some in Israel, where Azaria’s case had been taken up by the political right.

For human rights watchers, it is a worrying development. “The president’s decision is a clear demonstration that the Israeli justice system is neither willing nor able to enforce the law against soldiers who harm Palestinians,” noted Ziv Stahl, director of the Israeli human rights group Yesh Din.
However unequal that may appear to critics now, it is a trend with precedents reaching back to Israel’s founding.

During the Arab-Israeli war between 1947 and 1949, some 750,000 Palestinians were uprooted from their homes. It was an expulsion that could not have happened without extreme violence, including dozens of massacres by Zionist militias and Israeli army.
The perpetrators were rarely, if ever, punished.

In November 1948, though, Israeli soldiers killed civilians in Hula, a village in Lebanon. This time, the direct commander of the operation arrested the officer who ordered the massacre and complained about him. An Israeli military court convicted company commander Shmuel Lahis of murdering 15 people and sentenced him to seven years in prison.
On appeal, his sentence was reduced to one year. Israel’s first president, Chaim Weizmann, then canceled his prison sentence in 1950.

Five years later, President Yitzhak Ben-Zvi pardoned Lahis. Decades later, in 1978, Lahis was appointed director general of the Jewish Agency, the primary Zionist organization promoting Jewish immigration and settlement in Israel.
These were distinct decisions, but together they show how a conviction for murdering Arab civilians eventually lost its practical and lasting consequences.

The Lahis case nevertheless established an early precedent for leniency toward an Israeli soldier convicted of murdering Arab civilians. It continued in the years that followed, when Israel, for several years after its independence, pursued an unofficial policy of shooting Palestinian refugees who attempted to return to their homes, their land, or the property they had left behind. Costing the lives of thousands until the mid-1950s, this unofficial open-fire policy turned the new border into a lethal instrument for making the results of the expulsion permanent.
That precedent became clearer after the massacre at Kafr Qasim.

On Oct. 29, 1956, Israeli Border Police killed Palestinian citizens of Israel returning home to Kafr Qasim, a village 12 miles (19 km) from Tel Aviv. Authorities had moved the start of a curfew forward without ensuring that villagers working outside knew about it. In all, Israeli troops killed 47 people. In the trial that followed, eight troops were convicted of murder and sentenced to prison terms ranging from seven to 17 years.
The ensuing military trial produced a principle taught for decades later in Israel: Soldiers must refuse an order that is manifestly illegal.

What happened after the convictions is less often remembered. The prison terms were reduced on appeal and, for some, reduced again by the military chief of staff. In November 1959, President Ben-Zvi shortened the sentences of the last two men still in prison, Shmuel Malinki and Gavriel Dahan. Both were released by March 1960. Less than 18 months after sentencing, every person convicted in the main trial was free.
Kafr Qasim, thus, left two legacies: The court drew a boundary against unlawful killing while other state authorities sharply limited the consequences for crossing it.

The pattern did not end with those early cases. Since the first Palestinian intifada, or uprising, began in 1987, human rights organizations have documented how seldom investigations into Israeli soldiers’ killings of Palestinians resulted in prosecution.
